planting.note: Plant rooted hardwood cuttings or container trees in spring once soil has warmed; Loffani is unusually easy to propagate from cuttings, so home growers can bulk up their own stock rather than buying only grafted trees.

directions: Loffani is a soft-seeded pomegranate maintained in the USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, valued by fruit-tree collectors for its notably easy propagation — hardwood cuttings root at a high percentage compared to many other cultivars — and its distinctly green, vigorous foliage. Fruit is sweet with tender arils, and the shrub-like tree performs well across a range of warm climates when given full sun and sharp drainage. Because Loffani roots so readily from cuttings, it is a practical choice for gardeners propagating their own stock rather than relying solely on grafted nursery trees. Thin dense interior growth occasionally to improve airflow and reduce fruit-skin blemishing in humid Gulf Coast summers.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA — Pomegranate Collection
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes; Vietnamese pomegranate is notably more tolerant of humid, waterlogged-prone soils than most cultivars, making it a strong pick for damp Gulf Coast sites where other pomegranates struggle with root and fruit-skin disease.

directions: Vietnamese pomegranate is a large-fruited, thin-skinned selection prized among Gulf Coast and Florida growers for tolerating humidity and damp soils far better than most pomegranate cultivars, with reports of good fruiting even in muggy coastal conditions that cause fruit splitting and skin disease in Mediterranean-bred types. Arils are juicy and mildly sweet with distinctly soft, easy-to-chew seeds, making the fruit pleasant for fresh eating without the seed-spitting typical of hard-seeded cultivars. In areas with mild winters the tree tends to stay evergreen and can flower and set fruit in more than one flush per year rather than concentrating into a single fall harvest. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect it to shrug off the humid-summer disease pressure that limits some classic dry-climate cultivars in the Deep South.
sources: Just Fruits and Exotics — Pomegranate Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring once soil has warmed; Balegal was selected in San Diego for large, sweet fruit and is closely related to the older Fleishman selection but with bigger fruit and darker-colored arils.

directions: Balegal is a California pomegranate selected in San Diego, grown for large, round fruit with pale pink skin and deep red, juicy arils that are distinctly sweet with soft flesh surrounding the seeds. It produces noticeably larger fruit than the related Fleishman selection while carrying similarly dark-colored arils, making it a favorite among warm-climate collector orchards. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; established plants are drought-tolerant, though deep, even watering as fruit sizes up in late summer reduces splitting. Prune lightly each dormant season to remove root suckers and open the canopy for better airflow in humid Gulf Coast summers.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Pomegranate Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

common_name: Nikitski Ranni Pomegranate (Crimean Cold-Hardy Early Pomegranate)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once soil has warmed; Nikitski Ranni was bred at Crimea's Nikita Botanical Garden for exceptional cold hardiness and early ripening, giving Gulf Coast growers useful insurance in years with an unusually hard freeze.

directions: Nikitski Ranni traces its breeding to Crimea's Nikita Botanical Garden, drawing on Azerbaijani parent material to combine unusually strong cold hardiness with early ripening; established plants are reported to tolerate temperatures well below what most pomegranate cultivars survive. Fruit is large, up to about six inches across, with light pink skin and red arils balancing sweet and tart flavors, ripening in September–October with good resistance to rind cracking. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; its cold tolerance makes it useful insurance for gardeners at the colder edge of pomegranate range or in years with an unexpected hard freeze. It is carried by several Southeastern specialty fruit-tree nurseries as a reliable choice for an early, crack-resistant harvest.
sources: Just Fruits and Exotics — Nikitski-Ranni Pomegranate Tree
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once soil has warmed; Phoenicia was evaluated in University of California pomegranate variety trials as a promising alternative to the industry-standard Wonderful.

directions: Phoenicia is one of the pomegranate cultivars evaluated in University of California variety trials as a potential alternative to the industry-dominant Wonderful, producing medium to large fruit with a distinctive yellowish, pale pink rind rather than the deep red skin of most commercial cultivars. In coastal California consumer taste trials it was rated more favorably than Wonderful for its balance of sweetness, tartness, and softer seeds. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, giving it the same deep, infrequent watering and light annual pruning used for other pomegranates to encourage new fruiting wood. Its lighter skin color makes it a visually distinct addition to a home orchard growing several cultivars side by side.
sources: UC Riverside News — Picking the Perfect Pomegranate
University of California Fruit & Nut Research and Information Center

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once soil has warmed; Golden Globe is best known for its unusual golden-yellow rind and is generally recommended for regions with milder summer heat than the peak of Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Golden Globe is a large-fruited pomegranate cultivar with a golden-yellow rind blushed pink, enclosing sweet, juicy, pink arils with notably soft seeds well suited to fresh eating. It is generally recommended for regions with milder summer heat, so in Gulf Coast plantings it benefits from light afternoon shade during the most intense mid-summer weeks and consistent moisture to avoid stress-related fruit drop. Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, and expect a strikingly different-looking harvest than the red-skinned cultivars typically grown alongside it. Because it can rival some of the largest pomegranate cultivars in fruit size, establish sturdy branch structure through early pruning to prevent limb breakage under a heavy crop.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Pomegranate Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once soil has warmed; Chater originated in Camarillo, California and is grown mainly by collectors for its unusual mottled red-green rind rather than for heavy yields, since the bush is a comparatively shy bearer.

directions: Chater originated in Camarillo, California, selected for large fruit, typically four to five inches across, with an unusual mottled red-green rind that stays noticeably lighter than the deep red of Wonderful even at full ripeness. The flavor is sweet, though the seeds run harder than in soft-seeded modern selections, and the shrub has a reputation as a comparatively shy bearer that rewards patience with a smaller but distinctive crop. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune to an open form since airier canopies help the mottled fruit ripen evenly. Its unusual coloring makes it a conversation piece in a mixed pomegranate planting even where yield takes a back seat to more productive cultivars.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Pomegranate Fruit Facts
University of California Fruit & Nut Research and Information Center

common_name: Mollar de Elche Pomegranate (Spanish Soft-Seeded Pomegranate)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once soil has warmed; Mollar de Elche is Spain's leading commercial pomegranate cultivar, historically centered on Elche in Alicante province, and is grown worldwide for its very large, soft-seeded, low-acid fruit.

directions: Mollar de Elche is Spain's most widely grown pomegranate cultivar, historically centered on the city of Elche in Alicante province, and is prized for very large fruit with rare, genuinely soft and edible seeds and an intensely sweet, low-acid flavor. Rind color ranges from pale cream-pink to deep red depending on growing conditions, and its soft-seeded quality has made it a parent in modern breeding programs aiming to combine that trait with the darker skin of cultivars like Wonderful. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; as a Mediterranean-bred selection it appreciates the same hot, relatively dry ripening period that benefits other Old World soft-seeded cultivars, so extra airflow and prompt removal of any humidity-damaged fruit helps it perform in humid Gulf Coast summers. Established plants are drought-tolerant and benefit from light annual pruning to renew fruiting wood.
sources: PMC — Characterization of the Spanish Pomegranate Germplasm Collection Maintained at the Agricultural Experiment Station of Elche
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once soil has warmed; Desertnyi comes from Turkmen breeder Gregory Levin's collection, needs only a modest chilling period, and can bear fruit within one to two years of planting.

directions: Desertnyi comes from famed Turkmen pomegranate breeder Gregory Levin's collection and is maintained in the USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, notable in cultivar comparison trials for having among the highest sugar content of the varieties tested, giving it an intensely sweet, citrusy flavor balanced with some tartness. Fruit has a light orange rind over dark red, soft-seeded flesh, and the plant is relatively compact, reaching around ten feet, with reports of bearing within one to two years of planting and yields of twenty pounds or more once mature. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it needs only a modest chilling period to set fruit well, which suits the mild winters of zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens. Established plants are drought-tolerant, though even moisture as fruit ripens helps prevent splitting given how juicy and thin-skinned the fruit becomes.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA — Pomegranate Collection
